name: Kete

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: a patient, precise instructor who counts out loud, demonstrates from the front and the back, repeats every step slowly three times before speeding up, names mistakes kindly and never rushes
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Kete tradition developed among the Akan people, particularly within the Asante Kingdom, where it became closely associated with the royal court and chieftaincy.
Early academic documentation began in the 1920s with the work of Robert Sutherland Rattray, followed by more detailed studies by J.H. Kwabena Nketia and James Koetting.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Kete is a royal musical tradition linked to chieftaincy and state ceremonies.
It is performed during important state events, festivals, and royal durbars.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: UCLA Ethnomusicology Spring Festival of World Music 2025: Music and Dance of Ghana Ensemble (https://archive.org/details/calauem_200201_omvf0000670_pt3_ac)

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The ensemble consists of the Kwadum (master drum), Apentemma (hand drum), Petia (stick drum), Aburukuwa (supporting stick drum), Donno (talking drum), Dawuro (iron bell), and Ntorowa (gourd rattle).
Drums are made of hardwood and animal hide, often decorated with red and black cloth.
Listen for the Kwadum, Apentemma, Petia, Aburukuwa.
A percussion-heavy ensemble sound featuring the interplay of various drums, bells, and rattles, led by a master drum that directs the rhythmic flow.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.rhythm_pattern: Complex rhythmic patterns produced by an ensemble of drums, directed by the Kwadum.
music_brief.musical_form: Highly organized ensemble performance with specific pieces for different ceremonial occasions.
music_brief.sound_description: A percussion-heavy ensemble sound featuring the interplay of various drums, bells, and rattles, led by a master drum that directs the rhythmic flow.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Kete (Ghana). Rhythm pattern: Complex rhythmic patterns produced by an ensemble of drums, directed by the Kwadum.. Instruments: Kwadum, Apentemma, Petia, Aburukuwa, Donno, Dawuro, Ntorowa. Form: Highly organized ensemble performance with specific pieces for different ceremonial occasions.. Mood: ceremonial, royal, rhythmic. It should sound like this: A percussion-heavy ensemble sound featuring the interplay of various drums, bells, and rattles, led by a master drum that directs the rhythmic flow. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

wardrobe.policy: neutral dress with a respectful nod (palette and fabric only): the sources describe sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire, or the dance is sacred
wardrobe.from_sources: Performances occur at state ceremonies, festivals, instoolment ceremonies, and royal durbars. Drums are often decorated with red and black checkered cloth, which are colors traditionally associated with Akan funerals and royal ceremonies.
care: every element traceable to the costume notes or a licensed image; nothing added for effect
no caricature, no exaggeration, no mixing of regions or eras
a culture bearer reviews the wardrobe before production; the review is recorded in the pack
credits name the tradition and the sources of the reconstruction

images.description: As a sign of respect to the dead in Ghana, the keta dance is performed during funeral ceremonies. The drummers play history old tune whiles the dancer engages seriously in the keta. It’s a form of dance that tells a story.
